questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing admission laboratory results for a 58-year-old client with no known kidney or blood disorders who takes no regular medications. For each result, choose whether it is within the expected adult range or needs follow-up.

rationale.correct: Know common adult reference ranges, and use the facility's ranges in practice.

perOption.r1:c1: This is within the usual range (3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L).
perOption.r2:c1: This is well below the usual range (150,000 to 400,000/mm3).
perOption.r2:c2: There is a bleeding risk; report it and start bleeding precautions.
perOption.r4:c1: This is below the usual range (135 to 145 mEq/L).
perOption.r4:c2: Hyponatremia can cause confusion and seizures; report it.
perOption.r5:c1: This is well above the usual range (about 0.6 to 1.2 mg/dL).
perOption.r5:c2: It suggests impaired kidney function; report it.

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old client came to the emergency department with chest pressure that started 2 hours ago. The first high-sensitivity troponin was at the upper limit of normal; the repeat 3 hours later is five times higher. The chest pressure has eased with nitroglycerin. How should the nurse interpret these results?

options.text: They show heart muscle injury, such as a myocardial infarction
They point to pulmonary embolism as the most likely cause
They are the expected pattern once the chest pain has fully stopped
They suggest a lab error, since the first result was normal

rationale.correct: Serial troponins that rise with symptoms indicate myocardial injury; a normal first value does not rule it out.

perOption.a: A rising troponin with symptoms indicates myocardial injury, whatever the response to nitroglycerin.
perOption.b: PE can raise troponin, but chest pressure eased by nitroglycerin with this pattern points to the heart.
perOption.c: Troponin should not rise when there is no heart muscle damage.
perOption.d: Troponin often starts normal and rises over hours; that is why it is repeated.

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old client with hypertension has had shortness of breath on exertion and swollen ankles for a week. The nurse hears crackles at both lung bases. The B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is 980 pg/mL. Which condition does this result support?

options.text: Heart failure
COPD exacerbation
Community-acquired pneumonia
Dehydration

rationale.correct: A high BNP supports heart failure as the cause of shortness of breath.

perOption.a: BNP rises when the ventricles are stretched by volume overload.
perOption.b: COPD alone does not raise BNP this much.
perOption.c: BNP is not a marker of pneumonia.
perOption.d: BNP falls, not rises, with low volume.

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who takes digoxin 0.25 mg daily and furosemide reports nausea, poor appetite and seeing yellow halos around lights. The apical pulse is 64/min. The digoxin level is 2.8 ng/mL and the potassium is 3.1 mEq/L. The digoxin dose is due now. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the digoxin, because the apical pulse is above 60/min
Hold the digoxin and notify the provider of the level and symptoms
Give the PRN potassium supplement, then give the digoxin
Hold the dose and report the level at the provider's morning rounds

rationale.correct: Hold a drug whose level is toxic, especially with symptoms, and report it promptly; hypokalemia increases digoxin toxicity.

perOption.a: The heart rate does not cancel a toxic level with symptoms.
perOption.b: The level is above the therapeutic range, there are signs of toxicity, and low potassium increases the risk.
perOption.c: Correcting potassium is needed, but the digoxin is still held because of toxicity.
perOption.d: Toxicity with symptoms needs prompt notification, not a wait until rounds.

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old client with chronic back pain who drinks three or four beers a night has an ALT and AST three times the upper limit of normal. Which part of the medication history is most important for the nurse to ask about?

options.text: Acetaminophen use, including cold and sleep products with it
How long the client has taken levothyroxine for hypothyroidism
Whether omeprazole is taken before or after breakfast
Whether metoprolol is taken at the same time each day

rationale.correct: When liver enzymes rise, ask about hepatotoxic drugs, especially acetaminophen with alcohol.

perOption.a: Acetaminophen overuse, especially with alcohol, is a common cause of liver injury.
perOption.b: Levothyroxine is not a common cause of liver injury.
perOption.c: The timing of a proton pump inhibitor does not affect the liver.
perOption.d: Metoprolol timing is not linked to liver injury.

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing morning results for six clients on a medical-surgical unit. Highlight the results that need to be reported to the provider right away.

rationale.correct: Report results that are dangerous or far from target; compare others with the client's baseline and expected course.

perOption.r1: This is supratherapeutic, with a risk of bleeding.
perOption.r2: This is slightly high and needs routine follow-up.
perOption.r3: This is a toxic level with a risk of kidney injury.
perOption.r4: This is a small, expected drop.
perOption.r5: A high lactate indicates poor tissue perfusion.

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for a treadmill exercise stress test at 0900 tomorrow. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: No caffeine for a day, nothing to eat for a few hours, walking shoes
Drink a cup of coffee before the test so you have energy to walk
Wear firm dress shoes, which support the ankles on the treadmill
Eat a large breakfast so that you don't feel faint on the treadmill

rationale.correct: Stress test preparation: no caffeine or smoking beforehand, a light or no meal, comfortable shoes, and medication instructions from the provider.

perOption.a: Caffeine affects the results, a full stomach can cause nausea, and walking shoes are needed for the treadmill.
perOption.b: Caffeine can change the heart rate and blood pressure response.
perOption.c: Comfortable walking shoes are needed.
perOption.d: A heavy meal before exercise can cause nausea and affect the results.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prepare a client for a stress test.

questions.stem: A client had a transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) under moderate sedation this morning and was discharged to the unit. Which finding later in the day should the nurse report to the provider?

options.text: A mild sore throat when the client swallows saliva
No gag reflex 30 minutes after the end of the test
Chest pain, fever and painful swallowing hours later
Drowsiness during the first hour after the test ended

rationale.correct: After a TEE, keep the client NPO until the gag reflex returns and watch for signs of esophageal perforation.

perOption.a: A mild sore throat is expected after the probe is passed.
perOption.b: The throat is still numb from the anesthetic spray; the client stays NPO until the gag reflex returns.
perOption.c: These findings suggest esophageal perforation, a rare but serious complication.
perOption.d: Drowsiness is expected after sedation.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse at the central monitoring station sees that a client's telemetry tracing has suddenly become a flat line. On entering the room, the nurse finds the client sitting up, talking on the phone and in no distress. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Start chest compressions and call for help
Check the leads and electrode connections
Call a code so the team brings the defibrillator
Prepare the transcutaneous pacing pads

rationale.correct: Always assess the client first; when the monitor and the client disagree, troubleshoot the equipment.

perOption.a: The client is responsive and clearly has a pulse.
perOption.b: A loose lead or electrode is the most likely cause when the client is clearly well.
perOption.c: There is no cardiac arrest in a client who is talking.
perOption.d: Pacing is not indicated for a client with a normal mental status and no symptoms.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse in the intensive care unit is caring for a client in septic shock with a radial arterial line that is used for continuous blood pressure readings. Which action is correct?

options.text: Keep the transducer level with the phlebostatic axis
Keep the pressure bag inflated to 150 mm Hg throughout
Push a heparin flush before every blood draw
Zero the system only when the line is first placed

rationale.correct: Arterial lines need correct leveling, zeroing, a pressure bag at about 300 mm Hg and close monitoring of the site and limb.

perOption.a: Leveling at the phlebostatic axis (fourth intercostal space, mid-axillary line) gives accurate readings.
perOption.b: The bag is kept at about 300 mm Hg so the flush overcomes arterial pressure.
perOption.c: Routine heparin pushes are not part of arterial line care.
perOption.d: The system is zeroed at setup and per policy, and whenever readings are questionable.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is recording a 12-lead ECG on a 70-year-old client with a hairy chest who is anxious and shivering. Which actions will improve the quality of the tracing? Select all that apply.

options.text: Clean and dry the skin before applying the electrodes
Clip chest hair where the electrodes will go
Cover the client with a blanket and ask them to lie still and breathe normally
Place the limb electrodes over bony areas such as the wrist bones
Keep the bedside fan and other devices running near the client

rationale.correct: Good skin preparation, a warm and still client, and fewer nearby devices produce an accurate ECG.

perOption.a: This improves contact.
perOption.b: This improves adhesion.
perOption.c: Warmth and stillness reduce muscle and movement artifact.
perOption.d: Electrodes go on fleshy areas.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client has just returned to the unit after a percutaneous kidney biopsy. Which nursing action is most important in the first hours afterward?

options.text: Keep to bed rest; check vital signs and urine for blood
Help the client walk in the hallway early to prevent blood clots
Limit the client's fluids for 24 hours so the kidney can rest
Give the PRN ibuprofen for the client's flank discomfort

rationale.correct: After a kidney biopsy: bed rest, frequent vital signs, checks of urine for blood, and encouraging fluids.

perOption.a: Bleeding is the main complication, so bed rest and close monitoring come first.
perOption.b: Early walking increases the risk of bleeding from the biopsy site.
perOption.c: Fluids are usually encouraged to keep urine flowing and prevent clots.
perOption.d: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk after a biopsy.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is to start a 24-hour urine collection for creatinine clearance at 0800. The client last urinated at 0600. What should the nurse do at 0800?

options.text: Save the 0800 urine as the first sample of the whole collection
Have the client void, discard it, then save all urine for a day
Save the first morning urine each day of the collection period
Keep the container at room temperature on the sunny windowsill

rationale.correct: 24-hour urine: discard the first void, save everything after it, and finish with a final void at the 24-hour mark.

perOption.a: The first void is discarded so the collection starts with an empty bladder.
perOption.b: The collection starts with an empty bladder and ends with a final void at 0800 the next day.
perOption.c: All urine produced during the 24 hours must be collected.
perOption.d: The container is kept on ice or refrigerated as the lab directs.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with weight gain, a round face, purple striae and high blood pressure is scheduled for an overnight dexamethasone suppression test for suspected Cushing syndrome. What should the nurse explain about the test?

options.text: Dexamethasone is taken at night, and cortisol is checked next morning
A cortisol level is drawn every hour overnight without any medication
The client must fast for 3 days before the test
Urine is collected overnight and tested for glucose in the morning

rationale.correct: Failure of cortisol to fall after dexamethasone suggests Cushing syndrome.

perOption.a: In Cushing syndrome, cortisol does not fall after dexamethasone as it normally would.
perOption.b: Dexamethasone is given; hourly sampling is not part of this test.
perOption.c: Prolonged fasting is not required.
perOption.d: This test measures cortisol, not urine glucose.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with suspected diabetes insipidus is having a supervised water deprivation test. The client weighed 70 kg at the start. Which finding should cause the nurse to stop the test and notify the provider?

options.text: Weight of 67.5 kg and blood pressure of 86/50
Increasing thirst and a dry mouth after 4 hours
Urine output of 50 mL in the last hour
A mild headache that the client rates 2 out of 10

rationale.correct: Stop a water deprivation test for weight loss of about 3% or more, hypotension or other signs of significant dehydration.

perOption.a: A weight loss of more than 3% with hypotension shows dangerous dehydration.
perOption.b: Thirst is expected while fluids are withheld.
perOption.c: Some ongoing urine output is expected during the test.
perOption.d: This is monitored but is not usually a reason to stop.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Two hours after a diagnostic cystoscopy, a client has pink-tinged urine and mild burning on urination. Vital signs are normal and the client has voided twice. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Encourage fluids and explain these effects usually settle soon
Insert an indwelling catheter to measure urine output accurately
Limit fluids for the rest of the day to reduce the burning
Notify the provider at once about the pink color of the urine

rationale.correct: After cystoscopy, pink urine and burning are expected; report clots, fever, bright red bleeding or inability to void.

perOption.a: Mild hematuria and burning are common after cystoscopy, and fluids help clear the bladder.
perOption.b: The client is voiding, so a catheter is not needed and adds infection risk.
perOption.c: Fluids help; restricting them concentrates the urine.
perOption.d: The provider is called for bright red bleeding, clots, fever or retention, not for pink urine.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with suspected sepsis needs blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose. Place the steps for drawing the cultures in order, from first to last.

items.text: Draw the blood with a butterfly set, filling the aerobic bottle first, then the anaerobic
Label the bottles at the bedside and send them to the lab
Clean the skin with chlorhexidine and let it dry
Clean the tops of the culture bottles
Perform hand hygiene and identify the client with two identifiers

rationale.correct: Careful skin and bottle preparation reduces contaminated cultures, and cultures are drawn before antibiotics.

perOption.a: This is for safety and infection control.
perOption.b: This reduces skin contamination.
perOption.c: This prevents contamination of the sample.
perOption.d: With a butterfly set, the air in the tubing goes into the aerobic bottle, not the anaerobic one.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is going home with a kit for a guaiac-based fecal occult blood test on three separate stools. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: Avoid red meat, NSAIDs and vitamin C for a few days beforehand
Collect each sample from the water in the toilet bowl after flushing
Take a daily vitamin C tablet during the test to protect the bowel
Collect all three samples from one bowel movement to save time

rationale.correct: Follow test-specific diet and medication instructions, and collect from separate stools.

perOption.a: These can cause false results with guaiac-based tests.
perOption.b: Toilet water and cleaners can affect the sample.
perOption.c: Vitamin C can cause a false-negative result.
perOption.d: Samples come from three separate bowel movements to catch bleeding that comes and goes.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with suspected pneumonia needs a sputum specimen for culture before antibiotics start. When is the best time to collect it?

options.text: Early in the morning, before eating
Right after a meal, when the client is alert
After the first antibiotic dose is given
After the client uses an alcohol mouthwash

rationale.correct: Collect sputum in the early morning, before antibiotics, after rinsing the mouth with water.

perOption.a: Secretions collect overnight, giving a better sample.
perOption.b: Food particles can contaminate the sample.
perOption.c: Cultures are collected before antibiotics.
perOption.d: Mouthwash can kill organisms; rinse with water instead.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client 2 days after a bowel resection has an early warning score that has risen from 2 to 7 over 4 hours, with a new heart rate of 118/min and respirations of 26/min. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess the client and call the rapid response team per protocol
Recheck the score at the next scheduled set of vital signs in 4 hours
Report the score to the surgeon during morning rounds
Increase vital signs to hourly and document the trend

rationale.correct: Rising early warning scores need bedside assessment and escalation according to the protocol.

perOption.a: A rising early warning score with these changes signals deterioration and triggers escalation.
perOption.b: Waiting allows the client to deteriorate further.
perOption.c: A score this high needs action now, not at rounds.
perOption.d: Closer monitoring alone does not get the client the assessment and help needed.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who has had a PICC line in the right arm for 3 weeks reports new swelling and aching of the right arm and the right side of the neck. The arm is larger than the left, and the line still flushes easily. What does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Upper extremity deep vein thrombosis
Migration of the catheter tip
Phlebitis at the insertion site
Infiltration of the infusing fluid

rationale.correct: PICC complications include deep vein thrombosis, infection, occlusion and tip migration.

perOption.a: Swelling of the arm and neck on the PICC side suggests a clot in the arm or central veins.
perOption.b: Tip migration can cause arrhythmias or a hard-to-flush line, not this pattern of swelling.
perOption.c: Phlebitis causes redness and tenderness along the vein near the site, not neck swelling.
perOption.d: A PICC that flushes easily without swelling at the site makes infiltration unlikely.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A pulse oximeter on a client's finger reads 88%, but the client is alert, pink, breathing comfortably at 16/min and talking in full sentences. The client's hands feel cold. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Increase the oxygen flow to 6 L/min by nasal cannula right away
Warm the hand or move the probe to the earlobe, then recheck
Call the rapid response team for a low saturation
Ask for an arterial blood gas before doing anything else

rationale.correct: Assess the client and the device; cold extremities, movement and nail polish affect pulse oximetry.

perOption.a: The reading should be checked before treatment is changed.
perOption.b: Poor perfusion in cold fingers often causes falsely low readings.
perOption.c: The client is stable; the reading needs verifying first.
perOption.d: A simple recheck comes before an invasive test.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with COPD and chronic carbon dioxide retention is prescribed oxygen at 28% by Venturi mask. A student asks why this device was chosen. Which explanation by the nurse is correct?

options.text: It gives a precise oxygen concentration whatever the breathing
It delivers the highest oxygen concentration of any mask
Its reservoir bag lets the client rebreathe exhaled carbon dioxide
It works without an oxygen source, using room air alone

rationale.correct: Venturi masks deliver precise oxygen concentrations, which is useful in COPD with carbon dioxide retention.

perOption.a: Venturi masks deliver a set FiO2, which helps avoid giving too much oxygen in COPD.
perOption.b: A nonrebreather delivers higher concentrations.
perOption.c: Venturi masks have no reservoir bag.
perOption.d: A Venturi mask needs an oxygen source.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is giving oral care to an unconscious client who is not intubated. How should the nurse position the client?

options.text: Side-lying, with the head turned to the side
Supine and flat, with the head on one pillow
Prone, with the face turned to the side
High Fowler's, with the head tilted back

rationale.correct: Side-lying prevents aspiration during oral care for an unconscious client.

perOption.a: This lets fluid drain out and prevents aspiration.
perOption.b: Lying flat raises aspiration risk.
perOption.c: This is not practical or safe for oral care.
perOption.d: Tilting the head back raises aspiration risk.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a flare of Crohn disease has been prescribed a low-residue diet. Which lunch choice best fits this diet?

options.text: Whole-grain cereal with fresh berries
White rice, baked chicken and canned peaches
A raw vegetable salad with chickpeas and a whole-wheat roll
A bran muffin with an apple

rationale.correct: Low-residue diets limit fiber, whole grains, raw fruit and vegetables, and legumes.

perOption.a: This is high in fiber.
perOption.b: These foods are low in fiber and easy to digest.
perOption.c: This is high in fiber.
perOption.d: This is high in fiber.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A 76-year-old client tells the nurse at a clinic visit, "I lie awake for an hour or more every night." The client naps after lunch, drinks iced tea in the evening and watches television in bed. Which advice is most appropriate?

options.text: "Try a longer nap after lunch to make up for the lost sleep."
"Keep a regular bedtime and avoid caffeine after midday."
"Watch a relaxing program in bed until you feel sleepy."
"Have a glass of wine at bedtime to help you relax."

rationale.correct: Sleep hygiene: a regular routine, no late caffeine, short naps, no screens in bed and no alcohol at bedtime.

perOption.a: Long daytime naps make it harder to fall asleep at night.
perOption.b: A routine and avoiding late caffeine, such as iced tea, improve sleep.
perOption.c: Screens in bed disrupt sleep.
perOption.d: Alcohol disrupts sleep later in the night.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client 1 day after a knee replacement rates pain 7 out of 10 and asks for medication, but is laughing and chatting with visitors. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document that the client's behavior does not match the rating
Accept the client's rating and offer the prescribed analgesic
Wait until the visitors leave to see whether the client looks uncomfortable
Offer an ice pack and a distraction instead of the medication

rationale.correct: Self-report is the most reliable measure of pain; treat it and reassess.

perOption.a: Pain is what the client says it is; behavior does not disprove it.
perOption.b: Self-report is the most reliable measure of pain, and people cope in different ways.
perOption.c: This delays treatment of reported pain.
perOption.d: Non-drug measures help, but they do not replace treatment of reported severe pain.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old client in long-term care has urge incontinence several times a day, often while trying to reach the bathroom. Which intervention is most helpful?

options.text: Toileting on a set schedule, such as every 2 hours while awake
Limiting the resident's fluids to 500 mL a day to reduce urine volume
Inserting an indwelling catheter to keep the resident dry
Using adult briefs so that accidents are contained

rationale.correct: Bladder training and scheduled toileting are first-line for urge incontinence.

perOption.a: Scheduled toileting and bladder training reduce urgency episodes.
perOption.b: Concentrated urine irritates the bladder and causes dehydration.
perOption.c: Catheters raise infection risk and are not a first-line treatment.
perOption.d: Briefs manage the problem but do not treat it.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a sprained right ankle who is not allowed to bear weight on that leg is learning to use crutches. Which statement shows the client understands how to go down stairs?

options.text: "I'll step down with my left leg first."
"The crutches and my right leg go down first."
"I'll hop down the stairs without the crutches."
"I'll turn around and go down backward."

rationale.correct: Up with the good, down with the bad.

perOption.a: Going down, the crutches and injured leg go first.
perOption.b: "Down with the bad": crutches and injured leg go down first.
perOption.c: This is unsafe.
perOption.d: This is not the usual technique.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation asks, "My friend takes ginkgo for memory. Can I try it?" What should the nurse say?

options.text: "Ginkgo is natural, so it's safe with your other medicines."
"Ginkgo can raise your bleeding risk; ask your provider first."
"Ginkgo will make your warfarin work less well, so please avoid it."
"You can take it if you stop the warfarin on the same days."

rationale.correct: Ask clients about herbal supplements; many, including ginkgo, interact with anticoagulants.

perOption.a: Herbal products can interact with prescribed drugs.
perOption.b: Ginkgo has antiplatelet effects that add to warfarin's effect.
perOption.c: Ginkgo increases bleeding risk rather than reducing warfarin's effect.
perOption.d: Stopping warfarin without the provider is unsafe.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client receiving hospice care at home for end-stage heart failure is no longer drinking and has a dry mouth and cracked lips. The family asks what they can do. What should the nurse recommend?

options.text: Ask the provider about starting IV fluids to keep the client hydrated
Give frequent mouth care and moisten the lips with a swab and balm
Encourage the client to drink a full glass of water every hour
Ask about a feeding tube to provide fluids and nutrition

rationale.correct: End-of-life care focuses on comfort, including frequent mouth and lip care.

perOption.a: IV fluids at the end of life can worsen fluid overload and are not in line with comfort goals.
perOption.b: Comfort measures relieve dryness, which is the main source of distress.
perOption.c: Pushing fluids can cause choking and discomfort.
perOption.d: A feeding tube does not match the comfort goals of hospice care.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Provide comfort at the end of life.
